prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: Somewhere

outputs.L1:
Somewhere in Kentucky, she went for kicks—  
spiked, polka-dot, mint-julep, Grade 1 stakes,  
white-gloved clubhouse how-you-do-sees—  
until all the horses broke their legs.

& for all the horses, my ex joined  
the Seine-et-Oise Thoroughbred Liberation Front,  
& she crashed all the Bentleys,  
& it was I who bled  
in Derby countryside, where horses  
die in Japanese slaughterhouses,  
defrocked of rose blanket & blue ribbon.

& how very they went  
into the kind of darkness knowing  
only My Old Kentucky Home—  
no longer a run for the roses; it’s besieged  
with cannibals & thieves.

& only Millionaires Row sings:  
a hero is a horse without a heart  
that never aches  
for lovers who cross them  
one too many times.

When we kill one horse, all of them die  
waiting,  
long after Kentucky.

& she slips white gloves on my hands,  
bent from carrying her on NYC streets  
jammed the wrong way in every direction.

How merry are we,  
how merry,  
how bright-shine beaming, no longer weeping.

& she bears my head to the heat,  
& I let it all go,  
& bet my last hat & home.

& how—  
& how very are we—

& it changes everything.
outputs.L2: In Kentucky, she chased thrills among mint juleps sharp with polka dots, a Grade 1 Stakes, white gloves, clubhouse greetings, and polite how-do-you-dos—until every horse shattered its legs. For their sake, my former lover enlisted in the Seine-et-Oise Thoroughbred Liberation Front and wrecked every Bentley, yet I was the one left bleeding across Derby country, where horses are stripped of rose blankets and blue ribbons and sent to die in Japanese slaughterhouses. How completely they vanished into darkness, remembering only “My Old Kentucky Home.” The Run for the Roses is no more; cannibals and thieves have surrounded it, while Millionaires Row alone keeps singing that a hero is a heartless horse, spared the pain of lovers who betray it once too often. Kill a single horse, and all horses perish, lingering long after Kentucky. Then she draws white gloves over my hands, warped from carrying her through New York City streets clogged in every wrong direction. How joyful we are—how joyful, how brilliantly radiant, no longer crying. She presses my head toward the heat; I release everything and wager my final hat and my home. How—how utterly we are—and everything is transformed.
outputs.L3:
The poem challenges the glamour associated with Kentucky horse racing by exposing the suffering hidden beneath its polished surface. Although the racing world is often celebrated for its beauty, wealth, and tradition, the poem focuses instead on the violence inflicted on the horses that sustain it. Their injuries and deaths reveal the moral cost of a culture that treats living beings as symbols of prestige and sources of profit.

This conflict becomes personal when the speaker’s former partner joins a radical thoroughbred liberation movement. By attacking symbols of wealth and privilege, the ex transforms concern for the horses into direct rebellion against the social order surrounding the racing industry. Kentucky’s romanticized traditions are consequently recast as part of a world under siege—one shaped not by elegance and honor, but by cruelty, greed, and betrayal.

The repeated claim that killing one horse means killing them all gives the poem’s protest a collective dimension. No animal’s suffering can be regarded as isolated, because each death represents the vulnerability of every horse caught within the same exploitative system. The refrain also suggests that grief spreads outward: the destruction of one life damages an entire community of animals and people.

In the closing scene, however, the poem moves away from accusation and violence toward tenderness and surrender. By allowing grief to be fully felt rather than resisted, the speaker is finally able to release it. This moment does not erase the suffering that has occurred, but it makes profound personal change possible, ending the poem with a fragile sense of transformation.
outputs.L4:
The poem dismantles the glamorous mythology surrounding horse racing by setting the spectacle of the Kentucky Derby against images of confinement, injury, slaughter, and grief. The race initially appears as a public celebration: a world of speed, wealth, ritual, and collective excitement. Yet the poem’s surreal, fragmented movement repeatedly exposes what that spectacle conceals. Horses emerge not merely as symbols of beauty and freedom, but as vulnerable bodies controlled by human desire, forced to perform, and discarded when they can no longer serve the industry. Images of liberation therefore remain inseparable from the threat of violence; every fantasy of escape carries the memory of captivity.

This conflict also shapes the poem’s treatment of a broken relationship. Public cruelty and private sorrow overlap, suggesting that grief cannot be divided into separate categories. The suffering of the horse, the failure of intimacy, and the speaker’s emotional disorientation become parts of the same moral landscape. The poem’s fractured images reproduce the experience of trauma: memories arrive out of sequence, beauty turns suddenly grotesque, and tenderness is interrupted by fear or loss. Rather than offering a stable narrative, the poem forces the reader to inhabit this instability.

At its center is the recognition that violence against a vulnerable being never remains isolated. To harm one body is to implicate the people who watch, benefit, remain silent, or accept the system that permits the harm. The poem thus expands individual suffering into a collective ethical crisis. Horse racing becomes more than a single industry or event; it represents the broader human tendency to transform living beings into objects of entertainment, profit, or emotional projection.

The conclusion, however, does not remain entirely within accusation and despair. It turns toward intimacy and surrender as possible forms of release. This surrender is not passive defeat, but a relinquishing of the need to dominate, possess, or control. By becoming vulnerable to another being’s pain, the speaker discovers the possibility of a different relationship to grief. Intimacy does not erase violence or restore what has been lost, but it allows sorrow to change form. The poem ultimately suggests that liberation begins when control gives way to compassion and when suffering is recognized as shared rather than private.
outputs.L5:
## Somewhere

Somewhere, beyond the noise of crowded streets and unfinished conversations, there is a quiet place waiting for us.

It may be a house beside the sea, where the windows are always open and the curtains move with the wind. It may be a bench beneath an old tree, a distant city glowing at night, or simply a room where we finally feel understood.

We spend much of our lives searching for somewhere else—somewhere kinder, brighter, easier. Yet sometimes, the place we seek is not marked on any map. It appears in a familiar voice, a shared silence, or the sudden realization that we no longer need to run.

Somewhere is not always far away.

Sometimes, it is here.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an experimental prose poem about the Kentucky Derby, horse racing, class privilege, animal cruelty, and a failed romance, using fragmented syntax and surreal imagery.
counterfactuals.output:
**THE FASTEST TWO MINUTES OF US**

At Churchill Downs the hats bloom first—  
orchids, satellites, small tax havens  
tilted toward the sun.

Below: the horses, lacquered weather.  
Muscle translated into money.  
Their eyes—two dark rooms  
where no one has asked permission.

You wore seersucker. I wore  
the debt of wanting you.

Mint crushed under ice.  
Sugar. Bourbon. Silver cups sweating  
like nervous heirs. Somewhere a trumpet  
unfolded its brass animal  
and the crowd rose, one enormous  
wallet with a mouth.

*And they’re off—*

A sentence fired from a pistol.

Hooves sewing the earth shut.  
Whip-flash. Foam. The bright silks  
of owners who have never carried  
their own luggage, never felt  
a bit bloom blood against the tongue.

You said love is a wager.

I said nothing, having already placed  
everything on your impossible name.

Around the final turn  
the horses became chandeliers falling  
through a mansion—  
crystal knees, electric lungs,  
the jockeys small prayers nailed  
to their backs.

One stumbled.

The band kept playing.

In the grandstand, a woman in pearls  
lifted her binoculars  
as if examining a distant war.  
A man laughed into his julep.  
The roses waited in their red arithmetic.

You kissed me only when the favorite won.

Afterward, behind the barns, dusk  
wore a veterinarian’s glove.  
A white screen went up—  
brief moon, portable mercy—  
and behind it the quiet machinery  
of consequence.

No cameras, please.

We left through separate gates.

Your limousine floated away,  
a black swan fed on gasoline.  
I walked past torn tickets,  
each one a little failed country,  
each one saying almost, almost.

All night the track circled my sleep.

The dead ran fastest.

The rich applauded forever.

And you—  
you kept rounding the bend  
in that ridiculous hat,  
carrying my heart under your arm  
like a trophy of roses,

like something beautiful  
bred to break.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a breathless, punctuation-light poem that begins “Somewhere in Kentucky” and blends mint juleps, Millionaires’ Row, injured racehorses, Japanese slaughterhouses, an anarchist ex-lover, and emotional release.
counterfactuals.output:
Somewhere in Kentucky  
the mint juleps sweat green moons  
along Millionaires’ Row  
while injured racehorses dream standing up  
their bright legs bandaged with silence  

and across the ocean  
Japanese slaughterhouses open at dawn  
steel doors breathing  
names becoming numbers  
muscle becoming money  

my anarchist ex lover calls from nowhere  
says every fence is a wound  
every finish line a lie  
then laughs like glass breaking  

I carry the sound into the grandstand  
I carry the horses the knives the crushed mint  
the hats blooming above old fortunes  
until my chest can hold no more  

and at last I let it go  
one long ungovernable cry  
racing past the rail  
past the roses  
past every hand that tried to own us
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a dark anti-Derby poem in a nonlinear stream-of-consciousness style. Include white gloves, rose blankets, blue ribbons, crashed Bentleys, cannibals and thieves, and the refrain-like question “how merry are we.”
counterfactuals.output:
**ANTI-DERBY**

how merry are we  
under rose blankets, sweating out the anthem,  
white gloves raised like small surrender flags—  
the horses have already fled the century.

Blue ribbons tighten around throats.  
Someone calls it tradition.  
Someone pours silver into silver  
while, beyond the hedges, crashed Bentleys  
cool in the rain like dead black beetles.

Begin again:

the finish line before the pistol,  
the stable after the fire,  
the winner born inside the photograph  
and nowhere else.

how merry are we

with cannibals and thieves in the royal enclosure,  
chewing the names from betting slips,  
stealing the teeth from luck;  
with roses pinned over bruises,  
with mud instructed to behave like velvet.

A trumpet. A fracture.  
White gloves applauding the beautiful machinery.  
Blue ribbons fluttering from an empty stall.  
The crowd becomes one mouth  
and the mouth asks for speed,  
asks for blood dressed as pageantry.

Yesterday arrives late,  
dragging a saddle through champagne.  
Tomorrow is a horse without a shadow.  
The present—  
a crushed hat beside the rail,  
hoofprints filling slowly with rain.

how merry are we

beneath rose blankets,  
beside the crashed Bentleys,  
among cannibals and thieves  
who toast the old gods of pedigree  
until every glass contains an eye.

No horse consents to the wreath.  
No field dreams of fences.  
Still the blue ribbons multiply,  
still the white gloves bloom  
over the wreckage—

how merry,  
how terribly merry  
are we.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a dense avant-garde love poem where horse racing becomes a metaphor for heartbreak and exploitation, moving from Kentucky countryside to crowded New York City streets and ending with the speaker betting everything and letting go.
counterfactuals.output:
Bluegrass morning—  
the hills wear dew like small, fraudulent diamonds,  
and you stand at the rail, beautiful as debt,  
while the mares breathe weather into the barns.  
A bell splits the pasture.  
Every heart is taught the same machinery:  
gate, whip, grandstand, ruin.

We loved in furlongs.  
You named my pulse *promising*,  
brushed the straw from my shoulder,  
checked my teeth for age.  
Behind us, Kentucky rolled its green currency  
under fences white as alibis;  
men in clean hats priced the thunder  
inside a body.  
Even tenderness had odds.  
Even your hand, stroking my neck,  
was measuring resale.

Then north—  
the long van of forgetting,  
the interstate cinched like a bit—  
until Manhattan rose,  
a thousand starting gates slammed upright.

Now cabs lunge yellow through rain.  
Turnstiles swallow the poor by exact change.  
On Seventh Avenue, everyone is running  
from a pistol no one admits was fired.  
Screens flicker: futures, favorites, bloodstock, weather.  
Your face appears in every black window,  
gone before I can lose it twice.

I follow the crowd to the underground book,  
where fluorescent light makes saints of no one.  
Men clutch tickets like eviction notices.  
A horse breaks down inside each silence.  
Somebody cheers. Somebody profits.  
Somebody draws the curtain  
and calls the curtain mercy.

What were we but a track  
built over softer ground?  
You rode me hard toward an invented finish,  
fed me sugar, sold my speed,  
left your silks hanging in my mouth.

Still—  
at midnight the city paws the pavement;  
steam lifts from its nostrils;  
sirens braid red roses through traffic.  
I take the last of my faith,  
the rent, the ring, the name you gave me,  
and lay them on the longest shot:

the dark horse with no owner,  
no papers, no wish to win.

The gates fly open.

I bet everything.

Then open my fist.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Produce a surreal political prose poem criticizing wealth and spectacle in thoroughbred racing, with compressed words, ampersands, minimal line breaks, violent equine imagery, and a strangely hopeful final line: “it changes everything.”
counterfactuals.output: The grandstand parliament glitters w/ toothmoney & champagne law, while silkbright heirs bet nations on a tendon’s whisper; downtrack the thoroughbreds—thunderveined, sugar-eyed—are whipped into advertisements, each flank a flag, each mouth a small red referendum against the bit. Billionaires rise like chandeliers applauding themselves. In the paddock, grooms stitch dawn to muscle, carry debt in their wrists, speak softly to creatures bred as futures & broken as facts. Then the bell—metal god—& the horses erupt, hoofbombs shredding the ceremonial grass, one falling where profit says no animal falls, its beautiful engine scattering silence through the hats. Cameras swivel away. Ministers grin. Odds bloom. But beneath the velvet arithmetic, the earth remembers every strike; beneath the earth, roots wager green against empire. A child at the rail refuses to cheer, opens both hands, & it changes everything.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
